turns.text: I remember the day my mother was forced out of our home. She was in her seventies, her back already bent, but you and your comrades made her wear that black sash, made her shuffle onto a packed bus with her head down, as if she was some criminal. You made her return to a village that never wanted her, just because her father had owned a little land. I stood at the window and watched her leave, clutching a cloth bag, shaking. At work, I spent hours reading your big-character posters, every wall covered with slurs and accusations, the air thick with the stink of glue and ink. My hands shook every time I picked up a brush, not knowing if today I would be called out, or if someone would drag me to the front for a struggle session. You turned my home into a place of fear. You turned my work into theater. You made us hide our family photos and burn letters. You did this, and the consequence was that I learned to never trust a neighbor’s smile, never speak freely at my own dinner table, never let my children see my real face. You call it revolution—I call it humiliation.

I remember those days, the way the air inside those apartments felt—tight, sour, like everyone was holding their breath. I was one of the ones who came to your building, yes. I remember the old women, the way their hands shook when we read out their names. When we forced your mother onto that bus, I stood at the stairwell, clipboard in hand, checking off names. I saw the cloth bag, the way she clutched it to her chest like a shield. I didn’t look her in the eyes. I kept my eyes on the paper, on the list. I told myself it was the right thing, that she was just going back to her roots, that she’d be safer away from the city. But I could hear her crying as she walked down the hall, and I tried not to listen.

The big-character posters—I helped paste some of those up. I remember the stink of the paste, the way the paper curled at the edges. I wrote slogans, sometimes I copied accusations from others. I watched people stop and read, their faces blank or tight with fear. I saw hands tremble, people looking at the ground. I told myself we were exposing hypocrisy, that we were tearing down old lies. But I also remember the silence that grew in those rooms, the way laughter disappeared, the way neighbors stopped talking to each other.

I did turn your home into a place of fear. I did that. I stood in the hallway and shouted slogans, and I watched people flinch. I saw the curtains twitch, the lights go out early. I remember the smell of burnt letters—once, when we searched another apartment, I found a pile of half-burned photographs, faces already eaten by the flames. I picked one up with my shoe and kicked it aside.

At the time, I told myself it was justice. Now, I think about the faces I saw lowered, the hands that shook, the way people stopped trusting even their own families. I can’t undo it. I can only say: I did it, I saw it, and it lives with me too.

You say you tried not to listen to my mother crying, but it was your job to make her cry. I watched you and your friends stand in the courtyard, laughing as you checked names, like you were handing out prizes. I saw the way you eyed our windows, daring us to look back. You talk about justice—what justice is there in forcing a seventy-year-old woman to walk alone down a muddy road, clutching her only coat, while you scribbled slogans about ‘class enemies’ on our front gate? At work, you made us stand for hours, reading out confessions that weren’t ours, while you Red Guards sat in the front row, arms crossed, waiting for someone to stumble over a phrase so you could shout them down. My legs ached, my mouth went dry, but I didn’t dare ask for water. We stopped eating together at home. My son hid his schoolbag because he was afraid you’d search it for ‘bourgeois’ books. My daughter cut her own braids off with sewing scissors, crying in the bathroom so you wouldn’t do it for her. You talk about silence—yes, you created it, but you also made us swallow our words until we forgot how to speak. Do you know what it’s like to hear your own child whisper, “Don’t tell anyone where Baba is”? That is what you gave us. Fear, and the habit of silence.

You say we laughed, and maybe some did—maybe I did, once or twice, when the nervous energy boiled over, when it felt like the only way to keep moving. But I remember the courtyard, the way the stone tiles felt slick under my shoes from the morning rain, the damp chill on my skin. The list in my hand shook sometimes, but I gripped it tight, like it was a shield. I remember glancing up at the windows, seeing faces behind the curtains, some pressed close, others hiding in the shadows. I told myself we were being watched by enemies, but I see now it was just frightened neighbors, trying to keep track of who would be next.

I remember painting those slogans on your gate. The brush was heavy with black ink, and my hand cramped from gripping it too hard. The characters ran in places, dripping down the wood. I wrote ‘class enemy’ in thick strokes, and as I did it, I felt a strange mixture—pride, yes, but also a kind of hollowness, like I was acting in a play and couldn’t step off the stage. I never thought about your mother’s coat, or how she’d walk that muddy road. I only cared that the slogan was visible, that the message was clear.

At the struggle sessions, I sat in the front row, arms crossed, just as you say. I remember the taste of dust in my mouth, the way the fluorescent lights flickered overhead, the sweat running down the faces of those forced to stand. I watched for mistakes, for hesitation, for anything that could be called out. I remember the relief I felt when someone else stumbled, because it meant the attention stayed off me. I never thought about thirst, or aching legs—I was too busy looking for signs of weakness, too afraid of being accused myself. I saw children with their heads down, clutching schoolbags. I saw girls with their hair hacked short, uneven, sometimes with blood at the scalp. I watched mothers press their hands to their mouths to keep from crying out.

You say you learned silence. I learned it too, in a different way. At home, I stopped speaking to my father after he was labeled. I hid my own schoolbooks, tore the cover off a Russian novel and flushed it down the toilet, afraid someone would find it. I told myself I was strong, that I was on the right side. But every time I heard a child whisper, every time I saw a family eating in silence, I felt something twist in my gut. I can’t give you back your words, or your trust. I can only say: I saw what we did, and I know the fear you describe. I carried it too, even as I was the one who made you feel it.

You say you carried fear too, but you carried it with power in your hands. I carried it as a mark on my back, one I could never scrub off. You had the freedom to choose who to accuse, who to spare, who to humiliate. I had to watch my children shrink into themselves, counting the seconds until your footsteps faded from the stairwell. You talk about your shaking hands and your guilt, but I still see my mother’s shoes—her only pair—splattered with mud when she came home, months later, after you’d broken her spirit and her health. She never spoke above a whisper again. My own voice still catches when I hear shouting, even now, decades later. My heart races when I see a red armband, even in an old photograph. That’s what you left us with: bodies that flinch at laughter, children who distrust their own parents, neighbors who never again shared a meal. You say you know what you did. I want to know: do you ever dream of the faces you watched crumble? Do you ever hear the silence you created, echoing back at you at night?

There are nights when I can’t sleep, and I see faces—blurred, sometimes, but always turned downward, shoulders hunched, backs bent. I see the hospital director’s face, red and swollen from shouting back at us, then silent as we forced him to kneel in the courtyard. I see the young nurse’s body, hanging from the pipe in the duty room, her shadow thrown against the wall by the yellow light. I remember the sound of her shoes thudding on the linoleum when we cut her down—how everyone went quiet, even the most zealous among us.

Sometimes, when I close my eyes, I hear the chants, the slogans echoing in the stairwell, but underneath there’s always another sound: the muffled crying, the shuffling of feet, the click of scissors as we hacked off hair. When I was ordered to shave that teacher’s head—when the old clipper pulled at her scalp and she screamed—I felt a kind of nausea, but I kept going. I told myself I had no choice, but the truth is, I didn’t stop my hand. I watched her face in the cracked mirror, streaked with tears and snot, and I turned away because I couldn’t look at what I’d done.

You ask about dreams: yes, I dream of faces. Sometimes I see my own father’s—after he was labeled, he stopped eating, stopped speaking. I watched him stare at the wall for hours, and I hated him for being weak, even as I feared I’d end up like him. The silence you talk about—it’s in me too. There are whole years I can’t talk about, not even with my own children. When I hear shouting in the street now, my body tenses, my palms sweat, and I feel fourteen again, waiting for someone to point at me.

I won’t pretend I suffered as you did. I had power, yes, and I used it. I watched people crumble. I saw the way a person’s spirit could be broken—not just by beatings, but by being forced to kneel on gravel, by having your life paraded through the streets, by losing the right to speak. I can’t claim innocence. I can only say the silence I created never left me, either. It sits with me, even when the world is quiet.
